claims.nodeLabel: The misappropriation allegation: Grusch's ICIG complaint and sworn testimony
claims.text: The named mechanism in the allegation is procurement rather than appropriation: 'illegal contracting against the Federal Acquisition Regulations' describes government money reaching a contractor under an instrument that does not comply with the rules determining what the government gets for it - which is the precise legal condition under which recovered material could sit in private custody while having been paid for with federal funds. Reasoning: the FAR governs data rights, property title and cost allowability; contracting outside it is how title would fail to pass.

edges.label: Serving NASIC officer corroborates on the record under pseudonym
edges.note: 'The non-human intelligence phenomenon is real. We are not alone.' A currently serving Top Secret-cleared NASIC officer would corroborate but would not attach a name - itself evidence about the environment at Wright-Patterson.

edges.label: Serving intelligence officer at NASIC, Wright-Patterson AFB
edges.note: Kean identifies Grey as a currently serving NASIC officer with Top Secret clearance; the installation is the historical center of gravity for every legacy custody allegation.

edges.label: Corroborates the existence of a class of well-placed sources; facilitated congressional briefings
edges.note: Grusch referred roughly 40 witnesses to the ICIG; Mellon independently states well-placed officials shared detailed information with him and has facilitated classified congressional briefings. Reasoning: the two streams are described separately in the same article, and no document establishes overlap - but they converge on the same committees.

b.label: FY2023 NDAA, Public Law 117-263 - Sec. 1673 (50 U.S.C. 3373b) UAP reporting/whistleblower protection; Div. F secs. 6802-6803 establishing AARO

edges.label: Helped draft the UAP whistleblower protection language
edges.note: The Debrief reports Grusch helped draft the UAP language in the FY2023 NDAA, signed December 2022, which permits authorized UAP disclosures without retaliation regardless of prior nondisclosure agreements - written by the person who would then need it.

edges.label: The named complainant, under oath and under an IG complaint
edges.note: Grusch filed the ICIG urgent-concern complaint in May 2022 through counsel, was found credible and urgent in July 2022, went on the record in June 2023 and testified under oath on 26 July 2023. Attested by The Debrief reporting and the House Oversight hearing record.

b.label: United States Department of Defense (secondary designation: Department of War)

edges.label: First protected disclosure to the DoD Inspector General, July 2021
edges.note: The Debrief records that Grusch provided classified information to the DoD IG in July 2021 regarding the concealment of UAP-related material from Congress, ten months before the ICIG filing. The reprisal complaint alleges his identity and those communications were later disclosed outside the IG channel.

edges.label: Corroborating NASIC officer sits at the installation at the center of the legacy custody claims
edges.note: Grusch testified he knows the exact locations of held material and provided them to the Inspector General; the one corroborator whose duty station is public serves at NASIC, Wright-Patterson. Reasoning: the geography is suggestive and no document places Grusch's locations at Wright-Patterson.

edges.label: The allegation of illegal contracting and the statute that names IR&D
edges.note: Grusch's on-the-record formulation was 'illegal contracting against the Federal Acquisition Regulations'; six months later Congress barred UAP-related IR&D from being an allowable indirect cost. The inference that the two describe the same mechanism is reasoned, not documented: no source states that section 1687(b) was drafted in response to Grusch.
